title: The Afternoon Brief: Camp injuries mount as FIFA rift and takeover collapse
dek: Training camp took a toll on multiple NFL and soccer rosters, three confederations representing 136 of FIFA's 211 member associations formally accused Gianni Infantino of deception, and a regulator-approved takeover of Derby County fell apart anyway.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: The day's throughline is institutions and rosters both absorbing setbacks that were procedurally cleared but still collapsed or worsened, from Derby's approved takeover to Hunter Greene's second elbow surgery of the year.
bottom_line: Tuesday's throughline continued into midday: formal approval did not prevent collapse, from Derby's regulator-cleared takeover falling apart to injuries mounting across NFL and soccer camps despite teams' own plans. New developments included Eagles pass rusher Jonathan Greenard's extended timeline, Barcelona forward Roony Bardghji's second ACL tear to the same knee, Reds pitcher Hunter Greene's season-ending UCL surgery, and Tim Anderson's retirement citing mental health. The FIFA confederation letter, representing a majority of the organization's member associations, and the WNBA's unresolved eligibility question both remain open institutional fights without resolution today. Watch official injury updates from Chicago, Detroit, and Philadelphia, September's FIFA-confederation discussions, and any formal WNBA policy statement.
body: The picture at midday is one of plans undone after clearing their formal hurdles. Turki Alalshikh's takeover of Derby County had already been approved by both the English Football League and the Independent Football Regulator, yet he withdrew Monday, citing insufficient time to prepare the club before the season's start. In soccer's governance fight, UEFA, Concacaf, and the AFC, representing 136 of FIFA's 211 member associations, a clear majority, issued a joint open letter accusing president Gianni Infantino of a fundamental breach of trust and deception over his failed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. Both stories share a pattern: formal approval or formal standing did not prevent things from falling apart.

On the injury front, the day added to Tuesday's toll rather than easing it. The Bears' Luther Burden III remains expected to miss the preseason with a groin injury, and the Lions' Cade Mays remains projected out 8 to 10 weeks with a wrist fracture, both as reported this morning. New today, the Eagles' Jonathan Greenard, acquired in April for two third-round picks and signed to a four-year, $100 million extension, will miss at least another couple of weeks with a pectoral strain, with defensive coordinator Vic Fangio expressing uncertainty about whether Greenard practices before the regular season. Barcelona forward Roony Bardghji tore the ACL in his right knee in training, the second tear to the same knee in two years, ruling out any transfer before the September 1 deadline. In baseball, Reds right-hander Hunter Greene will have season-ending surgery for a partially torn UCL, his second major elbow procedure of 2026, and two-time All-Star Tim Anderson retired from MLB at 33, citing mental health struggles.

Transfer business continued alongside the injury news. Liverpool completed a season-long loan of Barcelona defender Ronald Araujo with a roughly 55 million euro option to make it permanent. Fulham signed midfielder Shea Charles from Southampton for a reported £30 million, and Nottingham Forest added Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande from Sporting CP for a reported £34 million. The NFL, separately, updated its replay rule to let head coaches designate a staff member to throw the challenge flag, a change made without an ownership vote.

The WNBA's eligibility question, first reported this morning, also carried into the day's coverage. Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham told ESPN she wanted to protect young girls who she said should not have to compete against biological men, and separately said it was common sense to bar transgender athletes from women's sports; the reporting does not establish which statement came first. Her comments drew support from President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, and prompted Enes Kanter Freedom to declare himself a prospective 2027 WNBA draft entrant, testing the league's undefined eligibility language. Separately, DiJonai Carrington clarified her own social media comments following an ejection from a Sky-Fever game, saying she never claimed the foul call itself reflected white privilege.

Why these things happened varies by story. Alalshikh directly attributed the Derby withdrawal to the compressed timeline created by the season's start, not to any new obstacle in the regulatory process. The FIFA confederations frame Infantino's alleged deception as a breach tied to the compressed and unconsulted rollout of his privatization plan. The injuries across NFL and soccer camps are attributed to specific in-practice incidents (a red zone rep for Burden, a lift for Greenard, a training session for Bardghji) rather than any pattern the reporting draws out. On the WNBA matter, the reporting establishes what was said and by whom, not what the league intends to do.

What to watch in the coming days: whether Chicago or Detroit issue official injury timelines for Burden and Mays, whether Greenard practices before the regular season, and whether Bardghji's surgery outcome affects his 2026-27 availability. On governance, watch September meetings between FIFA confederations and U.S. Soccer, whether a formal challenger to Infantino emerges before March, and whether the WNBA issues a policy statement following commissioner meetings with team presidents. On Derby, watch whether Alalshikh revisits the deal, as he indicated he might.
